subject: dermatology
title: Port-wine stain and capillary malformation

steps.tx: A **port-wine stain** is a capillary malformation present at birth. Unlike an infantile haemangioma, it does not proliferate and does not spontaneously resolve. It is caused by somatic activating mutations, most often in GNAQ, which drive MAPK signalling in endothelial cells. The vessels are structurally abnormal and dilate over time, so the lesion darkens and thickens with age.

steps.tx: A facial stain in the **V1 distribution** (forehead and upper eyelid) raises concern for **Sturge-Weber syndrome**. This carries leptomeningeal vascular malformation, seizures, and **glaucoma**. Screen with contrast-enhanced brain MRI and ophthalmology review with intraocular pressure measurement. Look for tram-track calcification on imaging.
steps.say: A facial stain in the V1 distribution, meaning the forehead and upper eyelid, raises concern for Sturge-Weber syndrome. This carries leptomeningeal vascular malformation, seizures, and glaucoma. Screen with contrast-enhanced brain MRI and ophthalmology review with intraocular pressure measurement. steps.tx: Limb capillary stains that are geographic and well demarcated may signal an overgrowth syndrome, such as **RASA1** capillary malformation-arteriovenous malformation or a **PIK3CA**-related disorder. Overgrowth of soft tissue and bone can occur, especially in segmental facial or limb lesions. Monitor limb length and refer syndromic or extensive disease to a vascular anomalies team.

steps.tx: Do not confuse a port-wine stain with a **salmon patch** (naevus simplex), which is transient, pale, and often fades by about two years, except on the nape. A persistent, darkening stain is a port-wine stain and should not be reassured as self-resolving. Keep the **Sturge-Weber** screen in mind for any V1 lesion.
